0.0.n: Sets the time of the viewer’s recommendation in the past.

0.1.n: Adds a conversational pause and draws the listener in.

0.3.n: Refers to someone who watches the speaker’s videos.

0.4.n: Links 視聴者 to the respectful word 方, referring to a person who is a viewer.

0.5.n: A respectful way to refer to someone; 視聴者の方 politely means a viewer.

0.6.n: Marks the viewer as the person whose words the speaker gratefully received.

0.8.n: The name of a food delivery service, written in katakana.

0.9.n: Used to recommend the service; the topic marker after ウーバーイーツ is omitted.

0.11.n: Adds friendly assurance to the recommendation.

0.13.n: A casual quotation marker introducing what the viewer said.

1.0.n: 言って is the linking form of 言う; いただいた politely presents the telling as a favor received.

1.1.n: Introduces the recommendation as a reason for the speaker’s later action.

2.0.n: Refers to this particular occasion of ordering food.

2.1.n: Refers to the charge for having the food delivered.

2.2.n: Marks 送料 as what is free.

2.3.n: Describes the delivery fee as costing nothing.

2.4.n: Connects 送料が無料 to キャンペーン, describing a promotion with free delivery.

2.5.n: This borrowed word refers to a special commercial offer here.

2.6.n: Casual contraction of やっていた, describing a promotion that was ongoing.

2.7.n: Gives the free-delivery promotion as the reason for trying an order.

2.8.n: The name of a Japanese restaurant chain; here it stands for food ordered from that chain.

2.9.n: 頼んで is the linking form of 頼む; adding みた means trying the action.

2.10.n: Short for の, adding an explanatory tone to the account.

2.11.n: Makes the explanation polite after ん.

2.12.n: A softer, longer form of けど that leads into further comments.

3.0.n: A conversational filler that softens the transition to other food options.

3.1.n: Usually refers to bite-sized, seasoned fried chicken in this food context.

3.2.n: Marks fried chicken as one example in an open-ended list.

3.3.n: A food word borrowed into Japanese and written in katakana.

3.4.n: Marks pizza as another example without making the list exhaustive.

3.5.n: Used casually instead of すごく to intensify 美味しそう.

3.6.n: 美味しい becomes 美味しそう to express appearance; な connects it to もの.

3.7.n: Refers to available food options rather than objects in general.

3.8.n: Highlights the appealing options in contrast with what the speaker actually chose.

3.9.n: Past form of ある, saying those food options were available.

3.10.n: Short for の, presenting the available options as background information.

3.11.n: Adds politeness to the explanation formed with ん.

3.12.n: Signals a contrast between the appealing alternatives and the final choice.

4.0.n: Introduces the final decision after considering other options.

4.1.n: Points to the familiar reassurance associated with Matsuya.

4.2.n: Describes the comfort of choosing something familiar and dependable.

4.3.n: Marks 安心感 as the quality being described as exceptional.

4.4.n: Expresses a striking difference in degree, here praising Matsuya’s reassuring familiarity.

4.5.n: Connects the judgment 段違い to こと, packaging it as a reason.

4.6.n: Turns the preceding judgment into a noun-like idea within ということで.

4.7.n: Completes ということで, presenting the preceding judgment as the basis for the choice.

4.8.n: The restaurant chain’s name; the object marker を is omitted before 選んで.

4.9.n: 選んで plus しまいました suggests an eventual, perhaps predictable choice; the ending is polite.

4.10.n: Adds a reflective, conversational tone and invites shared understanding.

5.0.n: Part of casual ていうか, shortened from というか, used to shift or reframe a comment.

5.1.n: か completes ていうか; ね adds a friendly appeal to the listener.

5.3.n: うまい loses its final い before すぎる; the exaggeration expresses enthusiastic praise here.

5.4.n: Short for の, giving the praise an explanatory, emphatic tone.

5.5.n: Adds politeness despite the casual wording around it.

5.6.n: Emphasizes the speaker’s enthusiastic assessment for the listener.

5.8.n: Casual form of やはり, confirming the speaker’s established preference.

5.9.n: The first part of 牛丼, referring to the meat topping.

5.10.n: The second part of 牛丼; together the characters name a dish of beef served over rice.

0.lit: Previously, you know, from a viewer, “Uber Eats is recommended, I tell you,” that…
0.tip: って marks the quoted recommendation, while に identifies the person who gave it.

1.lit: Because I received the favor of being told,
1.tip: 言っていただいた respectfully frames someone telling you something as a favor you received.

2.lit: This time, because a delivery-fee-free promotion was running, I tried ordering Matsuya, but…
2.tip: A verb’s linking form plus みる means trying the action; 頼んでみた means tried ordering.

3.lit: Well, things like fried chicken and pizza, really delicious-looking things, there were, but…
3.tip: 美味しそう describes how food looks, not a taste the speaker has already confirmed.

4.lit: In the end, because this reassurance is on another level, I ended up choosing Matsuya, you know.
4.tip: ということで turns the preceding judgment into the reason for choosing Matsuya.

5.lit: I mean, you know, excessively delicious they are, I tell you, after all, beef bowls.
5.tip: 牛丼 comes last as an afterthought identifying what the speaker has just praised.
